records.label: drought
records.report:
Diagnosis: Drought

1. Leaf: The most prominent leaf shows a distinctive brown, crispy margin with a dull, matte texture, indicating water loss and tissue desiccation. The green inner tissue is still intact, but the margins have curled downward, a classic sign of moisture stress.
2. Soil: The upper 2-3 cm of soil appears light-brown and powdery, lacking the dark, evenly moist surface typical of well-hydrated soil. This suggests the plant has not received adequate moisture recently.
3. Stem: The stem is slightly limp and lacks the firm, upright posture expected in well-watered plants, indicating reduced turgor pressure.

Recommendations:
a. Immediately apply 1-2 L of water per plant, allowing it to soak to at least 5 cm depth, then repeat every 2-3 days until new leaves regain turgor.
b. Install a drip irrigation system or watering can with slow-release emitters to deliver consistent moisture without overwhelming the root zone.
c. Add a 2-3 cm layer of straw or shredded leaf mulch around the crown to retain remaining moisture and moderate soil temperature.

records.label: drought
records.report:
Diagnosis: Drought

1. Visible cues: The most striking symptom is the entire plant's wilted posture, with limp, downward-curling leaves that lack the typical glossy green sheen. The green sepals on the top of the strawberry fruit indicate moisture loss and early leaf desiccation. The soil surface appears light-colored and cracked, lacking the dark, even moisture layer usually seen around the roots.
2. Recommendation: Immediately apply a deep soaking of 2–3 cm (about 1 in) of water, allowing it to penetrate at least 10 cm (4 in) into the root zone, then repeat every 3–4 days until normal leaf turgor returns. Add a 2–3 cm layer of straw or shredded bark mulch around the plant to reduce evaporation and keep the soil evenly moist. If midday temperatures exceed 30 °C (86 °F), set up a shade cloth providing 30–40 % shade during the hottest six hours of the day.

By these steps, the plant should regain its upright stance, and new leaves should regain their firmness within 3–5 days. Continual monitoring of soil moisture with a probe or finger test will confirm the mulch is effective and adjust watering accordingly. Additionally, ensure at least 20 cm (8 in) of clear space around each plant to improve airflow and reduce heat buildup.

records.label: drought
records.report:
Diagnosis: Drought

Visible cues:

1. Wilted, limp leaf with a pale yellow-green color, indicating loss of turgor and water deficit.
2. Small, shriveled calyx (green sepals) on the top of the fruit, showing the plant's last attempt to retain moisture in the developing berry.
3. Fine, downward-curling margins on the leaf edge, a sign of dehydration stress that can lead to further leaf drop if water is not restored.
4. Dry, dull surface of the stem, lacking the usual plump, glossy texture, which suggests the plant is not receiving enough water to sustain cellular turgor.

Recommendation: Immediately apply a deep soaking of 2–3 cm (about 1 inch) of water around the root zone, ensuring the soil is moist but not waterlogged, and repeat every 3–4 days until new leaves regain firmness. Add a 5 cm (2 inch) layer of straw or shredded bark mulch around the plant to reduce evaporation and keep the soil cooler. If midday temperatures exceed 30 °C (86 °F), set up a shade cloth or move the plant to a shaded area for the hottest part of the day. Over the next 7 days, check soil moisture daily by inserting a finger 5 cm (2 inches) deep and confirm it feels cool and damp, and watch for the leaf edges to regain turgor and for new berries to swell and darken without further shriveling.

records.label: drought
records.report:
Diagnosis: Drought

1. Visible cues: The most striking symptom is the widespread wilting and curling of the green leaves, indicating severe water loss. The leaf margins are curled downward and the leaf surface appears dull and limp, rather than firm and upright. The stems and petioles also show a similar loss of turgor, hanging limply instead of standing upright. These dehydration signs are most pronounced on the outer leaves, suggesting the plant is prioritizing foliage retention over water conservation.
2. Recommendation: Immediately apply a deep soaking of 2–3 cm (about 1 in) of water around the root zone, ensuring the soil is moist but not waterlogged. Add a 3 cm (1¼ in) layer of straw or pine needle mulch to reduce evaporation and promote even moisture release. Over the next seven days, irrigate to the soil depth of 5 cm (2 in) every other morning, adjusting frequency if the top 2 cm of soil feels dry to the touch. Increase airflow by spacing the plant 20 cm (8 in) apart to reduce heat buildup and improve uptake of available moisture.
3. Note that the green sepals at the top of the fruit cluster remain turgid and green, indicating the plant is prioritizing fruit development over leaf growth. However, the calyx edges show slight browning, a subtle sign of early water stress that can worsen if conditions remain dry. Maintain this watering schedule and monitor leaf turgor daily to catch any worsening of wilting or new browning before it spreads further.

records.label: drought
records.report:
Diagnosis: Drought

Visible symptoms on the visible parts:

1. Leaf blades are curled, limp, and have a dull, gray-green color, indicating loss of turgor and water stress.
2. The green calyx on the top of each strawberry is shriveled and curled back, showing moisture loss and early fruit dehydration.
3. The berries themselves appear small, under-ripe, and slightly shrunken, with a matte, non-glossy surface that signals insufficient sugar production.
4. The overall plant posture is drooping and lacking the crisp, upright turgor expected in well-hydrated strawberries.

These visual cues point to insufficient water uptake and excessive transpiration, which are classic signs of drought in strawberry plants. To alleviate this, immediately increase irrigation to a deep soak of 2–3 cm (≈1 in) every 48 hours, ensuring water penetrates at least 10 cm (4 in) into the root zone; additionally, install a 15% shade cloth during the hottest part of the day to reduce evaporation. Maintain this schedule until new, firm leaves emerge and berries regain normal size and sheen.

records.label: drought
records.report:
Diagnosis: Drought

Symptoms visible on the strawberry plant are:

1. Wilted, limp leaves with a pale green to yellowish hue, indicating loss of turgor due to reduced water uptake.
2. Dry, crusty soil surface with no visible moisture patches, confirming inadequate irrigation.
3. Wilting of the central flower, where the yellowed, drooping petals indicate dehydration and reduced bloom.
4. Leaf edges are curled downward and slightly curled inward, a sign of stress caused by low humidity.
5. Stem appears thin and slightly translucent, suggesting water deficit.

Drought is the most likely cause of these symptoms, so the recommended action is to provide deep watering immediately, aiming for about 2.5 cm (1 in) of water applied around the root zone every 2-3 days, ensuring moisture penetrates at least 10 cm (4 in) into the soil. Add a 3 cm (1.2 in) layer of straw or shredded bark mulch around the plant to reduce evaporation and improve soil insulation. Position a small fan or misting system to maintain at least 20 cm (8 in) of airflow around the plant to reduce surface heat and speed recovery. Over the next 7 days, check soil moisture daily by inserting a finger 5 cm (2 in) deep and confirm it feels cool and damp, watch for new leaves regaining firmness and a brighter green color, and inspect the soil surface each morning for any top layer drying before the next watering.

records.label: drought
records.report:
Diagnosis: Drought

Visible cues:

1. Leaf blades are curled downward and have a dull, matte green color with irregular margins, indicating water loss and stomatal closure.
2. Soil surface appears light-brown and powdery, lacking the dark, moist sheen typical of well-hydrated soil.
3. Stem tissue along the edges of the canopy shows slight wilting and a pale yellow hue.

These visual signs point to insufficient soil moisture, causing the plant to conserve water by reducing leaf turgor and delaying stem growth. Immediately apply a deep irrigation of 2.5 cm (1 in) of water, ensuring penetration to at least 10 cm (4 in) depth, and repeat every 3-4 days for the next week. Add a 3 cm (1.2 in) layer of straw or shredded bark mulch around each crown to retain moisture and moderate soil temperature. Position a 30 % shade cloth 40 cm (16 in) above the plant during the hottest afternoon hours to reduce further water loss. Over the next 7 days, check each morning whether the top 2 cm (0.8 in) of soil stays cool and damp to the touch, observe if new leaves regain upright posture by day 3, and verify that no additional leaf edges brown or crisp.

records.label: frost
records.report:
Diagnosis: Frost Injury

Visible cues on the strawberry fruit indicate a classic pattern of Frost Injury, with multiple areas showing a distinctive "frost-dried" texture and a dull, water-soaked sheen. The calyx (the green, cup-shaped structure at the blossom end) is blackened and browned, while the upper side of the berry shows a translucent, slightly sunken zone that has lost its normal glossy red color. The leaf visible at the top is also curled and edged with a pale, necrotic band, confirming that the injury extended to the leaf tissue as well. No flowers or green stem are visible in this image, so those structures remain intact and unaffected by frost.

records.label: frost
records.report:
Diagnosis: Frost Injury

Visible cues:

1. Frost-discolored, bronze-red petals around the yellow center of the flower, indicating tissue death from cold exposure.
2. Frost-crusted, translucent edges of the green leaf blades, with some margins turning translucent and papery.
3. Soil surface appears dark and unblemished, indicating the damage is localized above-ground.
4. Stem segments remain green but may show slight wilting and translucent patches where buds meet the stem.

Recommendation:

1. Immediately cover exposed plants with a breathable fabric or lightweight row cover before temperatures drop below 2°C (36°F) to reduce further cellular injury.
2. Apply a 5 cm (2 in) layer of clean straw mulch around each crown to insulate roots and moderate soil temperature.
3. Ensure drainage by lifting the mulch edge 5 cm (2 in) away from stems to prevent rot. Water plants in the early morning with 2 cm (¾ in) of water before sunset on cold nights to reduce further moisture loss.

records.label: frost
records.report:
Diagnosis: Frost Injury

Visible cues:

1. Frost-discoloration: Large areas of the leaf and stem show a pale, bluish-gray cast, indicating tissue death from exposure to sub-freezing temperatures.
2. Frost crystals: Small white crystals are visible on the upper surfaces of the leaves and stem, especially where they meet the soil, indicating rapid freezing of moist cells.
3. Flaccid texture: The leaf edges appear limp and slightly curled downward, a sign of cellular collapse caused by ice formation in the epidermis.
4. Faint brown margins: Some margins of the leaves show a darker, scorched look, suggesting the freezing front burned the outer cells.

Recommendation:

1. Immediately cover exposed plants with a breathable fabric or light fleece each evening when temperatures are forecast to drop below 2°C (35°F) to prevent further freeze damage.
2. Apply a 5 cm (2 in) layer of straw or pine-needle mulch around the crown to insulate roots and reduce radiative heat loss.
3. Delay morning irrigation until temperatures rise above 5°C (41°F) to minimize the risk of water freezing on the leaves. Instead, water in the early afternoon when air is warmer.

records.label: frost
records.report:
Diagnosis: Frost Injury

Visible cues:

1. Frost-discolored, mottled red and white berries, particularly on the upper halves, indicating tissue death from cold exposure.
2. Edges of the green leaves show dark brown to black necrotic patches, with intact green centers, a classic sign of frost desiccation.
3. The calyx of each strawberry is bright green and slightly puckered, suggesting cell collapse rather than full blossom drop.

Recommendation:

Immediately cover exposed plants with a breathable fabric or lightweight fleece before the next predicted frost, ensuring the material drapes 10-15 cm (4-6 in) beyond the crown to prevent radiant heat loss. Water the soil to a depth of 5 cm (2 in) in the early afternoon on the day before a frost to release latent heat, then withhold irrigation until daytime temperatures rise above 0 °C (32 °F). Remove any dead or damaged fruitlets with sanitized shears to reduce inoculum and improve airflow. Over the next week, monitor daily canopy temperature with a thermometer, protect buds with a 2 cm (¾ in) layer of straw mulch if temperatures dip below 2 °C (36 °F), and prune excess leaves to maintain a 30 cm (12 in) open center for better ventilation.

3. Ensure good airflow by pruning any encroaching foliage and keeping a 10 cm (4 in) gap between crowns to speed overnight thawing.

records.label: frost
records.report:
Diagnosis: Frost Injury

Visible cues:

1. Frost-discolored, bronze-to-gray blotches cover the upper leaf surface, particularly along the serrated margins, indicating tissue death from cold stress.
2. The green, downward-curling leaf blade shows a distinct line where the damaged tissue meets the still-green lower leaf, indicating a localized freeze burn.
3. The stem appears slightly darkened and water-soaked at the intersection with the leaf, suggesting the plant's vascular tissue was damaged during the freeze event.

Recommendation:

1. Immediately provide 2–3 cm (about 1 in) of overhead irrigation to release stored heat and rehydrate the plant, repeating every 8 hours until daytime temperatures exceed 10 °C (50 °F).
2. Apply a 2 cm (¾ in) layer of clean straw or pine-needle mulch around the crown to insulate roots and reduce future freezing.
3. Install a floating row cover or lightweight fleece (50 g/m²) over the bed each evening when forecasts predict temperatures below 4 °C (39 °F), holding it 10 cm (4 in) above the foliage to trap radiant heat.
4. Prune and discard any severely blackened or fallen leaves to reduce infection points and improve airflow. Ensure the removed debris is removed from the bed to prevent fungal growth.

records.label: frost
records.report:
Diagnosis: Frost Injury

Visible cues: The majority of the leaf blades display a distinctive dark-brown, glassy edge, indicating Frost-induced necrosis; many leaf serrations are crisply blackened and curled downward; and the soil surface remains powdery white where the foliage meets it, indicating rapid freeze-thaw desiccation. No Frost-resistant buds or new growth are visible, confirming the injury occurred during the recent cold event. These symptoms point to overnight temperatures dropping below 0°C, causing water inside the leaf cells to freeze and rupture cell membranes.

Recommendation: Immediately cover exposed plants with a breathable Frost cloth or straw mulch 30 cm deep each evening when forecasts predict temperatures below 2°C; ensure soil moisture is kept at about 5 cm depth by irrigating early in the afternoon, then allowing it to freeze only briefly; and install a low-emission heating mat or Frost-protective film around the crown zone to maintain 1–2°C above ambient. Remove any dead or damaged leaves with sterile scissors to reduce pathogen entry points and improve airflow. Over the next seven days, check each morning for new blackened margins spreading inward, confirm soil temperature with a probe reaches 5°C before sunrise, and verify that emerging buds remain firm and green rather than turning brown or mushy.

records.label: gray_mold
records.report:
Diagnosis: Gray Mold

• Fruit: Several gray, fuzzy growths cover the green calyx and part of the red achenes, indicating colonization on the surface. These tufts are soft, water-soaked, and slightly sunken, signaling fungal sporulation.
• Leaf: A pale yellow-green area near the stem shows a similar velvety growth, indicating infection spreading upward. The margin is slightly curled and edged with a faint brown ring, suggesting tissue degradation.
• Stem: The stem remains green, but the lower half is slightly water-soaked and has a few small, darkened lesions, suggesting internal infection.

Recommendation: Remove and discard all visibly infected fruit and debris, cutting at least 2 cm below the infection point to prevent spore spread. Thin surrounding foliage to create a 5-10 cm air gap between plants for better airflow, and apply a 2 cm layer of clean straw mulch to keep berries off damp surfaces. Irrigate only the soil, not the plant, with 250 ml per plant every 3 days in early morning, ensuring foliage dries quickly. Over the next 7 days, inspect daily for new gray fuzz on calyxes, check the underside of leaves for tan spores, and verify that mulch remains dry to the touch; adjust watering or spacing if any of these signs worsen.

records.label: gray_mold
records.report:
Diagnosis: Gray Mold

• Fruit: Several brown, sunken lesions cover the calyx and upper third of the berry, with a dusty gray-white fuzz visible on the softening tissue. The infection starts where the calyx meets the fruit, indicating active fungal growth.
• Leaf: The green blade shows a water-soaked, slightly translucent band running along the margins, and some tissue appears darkened and curling downward. This edge collapse is a common early sign of fungal invasion.
• Root: No visible symptoms are visible on the stem, so the infection is limited to the crown and fruit.

Recommendation: Immediately remove and discard all visibly infected fruit and leaves, then thin surrounding foliage to create at least 5 cm (2 in) of open space between plants for airflow. Apply a coarse straw or pine-needle mulch 3 cm (1.2 in) deep to keep fruit off damp soil and improve drainage. Every morning irrigate only the soil, delivering 2.5 cm (1 in) of water at the base, and avoid wetting leaves. Over the next 7 days, inspect daily for new soft spots on calyces, check for a sour or earthy odor on the mulch, and verify that the top 2 cm (0.8 in) of soil dries within 24 hours after watering.

records.label: gray_mold
records.report:
Diagnosis: Gray Mold

• The most prominent symptom is a dense, gray-white fuzzy growth covering the entire receptacle of the rotting strawberry, indicating the fungal mat characteristic of this disease.
• The green calyx (the top part of the fruit) is water-soaked and turning brown, signaling the fungus's early invasion of the fruit tissue.
• Several of the nearby leaf serrations (the pale green edges) show slight yellowing and a slight curl, a common early sign of tissue dehydration that can allow the mold to gain entry.
• The stem remains firm and green, indicating that the infection is localized to the fruit and not spread to the vascular tissue.

Recommendation:

1. Immediately remove and discard the infected fruit and any debris within a 5 cm radius to prevent spore spread.
2. Sanitize cutting tools with 70% alcohol between plants to prevent cross-contamination.
3. Increase airflow by thinning surrounding foliage to create at least 10 cm of space between plants, and water only the soil, not the crowns, with 1 cm of water early in the morning to keep leaves dry.
4. Apply a 1 cm layer of clean straw mulch under the canopy to reduce soil splash and keep fruit off damp surfaces.

records.label: gray_mold
records.report:
Diagnosis: Gray Mold

• Fruit: Several berries show soft, water-soaked lesions with a distinct gray, fuzzy growth on the calyx and shoulders, indicating Botrytis infection. The affected areas turn pale green and begin to collapse, signaling tissue decay.
• Leaf: The upper leaf edge is brown and dry, with a slight translucent edge where moisture has been trapped, indicating early infection spreading upward.
• Stem: The stem shows darkened, water-soaked patches near the fruit, suggesting infection has penetrated the pedicel.

Recommendation:

1. Immediately remove and discard all visibly infected fruit and necrotic leaf debris, cutting at least 2 cm (¾ in) into healthy tissue to prevent spore spread.
2. Improve airflow by thinning crowded foliage to create a 5–7 cm (2–3 in) gap between plants, and angle any overhead structures so leaves dry quickly.
3. Apply a coarse-leaf straw mulch 3 cm (1¼ in) deep under the canopy to keep fruit off damp soil and reduce splashing. Every morning, inspect and remove any new gray fuzz or browning patches on stems and leaves, and re-thin any crowded runners to maintain a 10 cm (4 in) spacing. Over the next 7 days, re-check the calyx and underside of leaves for fresh gray growth, and verify that the mulch surface remains dry to the touch by midday.

records.label: gray_mold
records.report:
Based on the provided image, the following are the visible symptoms of gray mold on the strawberry plant:

1. Gray-white, fuzzy growth: A dense, powdery layer of spores is visible on the green calyx of the strawberry, indicating active fungal colonization. This growth is typically grayish-white and velvety, and it can spread quickly over the affected tissue.
2. Water-soaked lesions: The upper third of the strawberry fruit shows soft, darker red areas that have begun to translate into sunken, water-soaked patches, indicating tissue decay caused by the fungus invading moist tissue.
3. Slight yellowing: The leaf edges appear slightly yellowed and curled, a common sign of nutrient deficiency or stress that can make the plant more susceptible to disease.
4. Limited infection so far: While the calyx is heavily infected, the stem and main leaf remain relatively clean, suggesting that the fungus has spread from a localized wound or over-moistened area.

To address this diagnosis, recommend the following steps:

1. Remove and discard all visibly infected fruit and calyces, cutting at least 2 cm (¾ in) below the moldy area to prevent spore spread.
2. Improve airflow by thinning foliage to create a 10-15 cm (4-6 in) gap between crowns and removing any plastic mulch that touches the plant.
3. Water only the soil, not the leaves, with a slow drip irrigation that keeps the crown dry; aim for deep watering every 3-4 days, allowing the top 5 cm (2 in) of soil to dry before the next cycle.
4. Apply a 2 cm (¾ in) layer of clean straw mulch around the plant to reduce splash and keep fruit off damp soil. Over the next 7 days, inspect daily for new gray fuzz on calyxes, firmness of strawberry shoulders, and any fresh yellowing of leaves, adjusting airflow and watering accordingly.

records.label: gray_mold
records.report:
Diagnosis: Gray Mold

• Fruit: Several berries show a dense, gray-white fuzzy growth on the surface, especially around the calyx area, indicating active fungal colonization. The affected areas appear water-soaked and slightly sunken compared to the firm, glossy red fruit nearby.
• Leaf: The upper leaf edge shows a similar gray coating, with a slight translucent texture that suggests sporulation. The tissue beneath appears wilted and slightly brown, indicating infection progression.
• Stem: The stem near the blossom end is discolored to a dull yellow-brown, indicating capillaria penetration into the stem tissue.

Recommendation:

1. Immediately remove and discard all visibly infected fruit and leaves, cutting at least 2 cm (¾ in) below the infection point to prevent spore spread. Sanitize shears with 70% alcohol between cuts.

3. Apply a 1 cm (⅜ in) layer of clean straw mulch under the canopy to reduce soil splash and keep fruit dry. Water only the soil, not the foliage, to a depth of 2 cm (¾ in) every 3–4 days in the early morning, allowing surfaces to dry by midday. Avoid overhead irrigation entirely.

records.label: gray_mold
records.report:
Based on the provided image, the following are the visible symptoms of gray mold on the strawberry plant:

1. Gray, fuzzy growth: A dense, velvety layer of gray spores is visible on the green calyx, particularly where the flower meets the stem. This indicates the fungus is colonizing the moist, inner tissue of the flower.
2. Water-soaked tissue: The receptacle (the green, fuzzy part) is slightly soft and translates slightly toward a yellowish hue, indicating localized moisture damage that allows the fungus to invade.

4. Irrigate only the upper 1 cm of soil every other morning with a gentle hose, ensuring leaves and flowers dry within two hours; avoid overhead watering.
5. Sanitize shears with 70 % alcohol between cuts to prevent spore transfer. Over the next seven days, inspect daily for any new gray fuzz on calyxes, check that leaf surfaces feel dry within two hours of watering, and verify that mulch remains dry to the touch to ensure proper drainage and airflow.

Therefore, the diagnosis is Healthy.

To maintain this status, recommend the following:

records.label: overwatered

Diagnosis: Overwatering

Visible symptoms: The most striking feature is the uniformly dark, glossy, and compacted soil surface, indicating excess moisture has suffocated the plant's roots, preventing normal oxygen uptake. The top 2-3 cm of soil appear densely packed and matte-finish, while the soil-colored calyx tips are wilted and curled downward, showing loss of turgor pressure. These visual cues suggest the plant has been receiving more water than it can absorb, causing root suffocation and foliage wilt.

Recommendation: Immediately reduce irrigation frequency and depth. Water only when the top 2 cm of soil feel dry, applying about 250 ml per plant, and allow excess to drain fully. Add a 2 cm layer of coarse straw or pine-needle mulch to improve surface aeration without trapping excess water, and gently loosen the top 1 cm of soil to enhance airflow. Over the next seven days, check daily for: 1) soil color lightening to a lighter brown, 2) calyx standing upright and regaining green sheen, and 3) absence of new yellow or white fungal spots on the soil surface, which would signal recovery.

Over the next week, check daily that the soil surface feels dry to the touch before watering, watch for new leaves regaining upright posture, and inspect the crown area for any fresh brown lesions to ensure the plant is recovering.

records.label: root_rot
records.report:
Diagnosis: Root Rot

The most prominent visual symptoms are:

1. Wilting and browning of the leaf's upper surface, with a sharp boundary between green and yellow-brown tissue, indicating water-logged, oxygen-starved cells.
2. The crown (where stem meets root) is dark brown and mushy, showing extensive decay of the root system.
3. The root itself is visibly shriveled and blackened, lacking the usual white, fibrous texture, indicating rot.
4. The stem shows slight collapse and loss of turgor, another sign of root failure transferring water stress to the above-ground parts.

These symptoms point to root rot caused by poor drainage, overwatering, or fungal infection that starves roots of oxygen. Immediately remove the affected plant section, cutting at least 5 cm (2 in) back from the diseased crown, and replant in a raised bed or pot with a well-draining mix containing 30–40 % coarse perlite. Irrigate only when the top 2 cm (¾ in) of soil feels dry, applying no more than 250 ml (1 cup) per plant every 3–4 days, ensuring full watering without standing water. Add a 2 cm (¾ in) layer of clean straw mulch around the stem to keep it dry and improve airflow. Over the next 7 days, check daily for:
1. New green growth emerging from the crown as evidence of recovering root function. 2. Soil consistency at 2 cm depth—if it remains soggy, withhold water until it feels dry. 3. Any spread of brown lesions along the stem or leaves, which would signal continuing rot and require further pruning or repotting.

records.label: root_rot
records.report:
Diagnosis: Root Rot

1. Leaf: The upper leaf is wilted and curled downward with a pale yellow-green coloration, indicating root failure to supply water and nutrients. The margins are dry and crisp, confirming moisture loss.
2. Root: Several dark brown, mushy roots are visible near the crown, indicating decay and collapse of the root system. These roots are soft, water-soaked, and lack the firm, white texture of healthy roots.
3. Fruit: The green calyx remains intact, but the berry is shriveled and has a dull, grey-brown surface, a classic sign of fruit suffocation due to impaired root function.
4. Stem: The main stem is slightly darkened and brittle near the crown, suggesting water-logging and decay that can progress upward if not addressed.

Treatment steps:
a. Remove and discard all affected roots and leaves with a sterile cutting tool, cutting at least 2 cm (¾ in) beyond any mushy tissue to prevent spread.
b. Improve drainage by repotting into a well-draining mix (e.g., 50 % peat-free compost, 50 % perlite) and ensuring each pot has at least 10 cm (4 in) of clearance from the base.
c. Water slowly with 2–3 cm (1 in) of water every 3–4 days, allowing the top 5 cm (2 in) of soil to dry before the next irrigation, and never leave the plant in standing water.
d. Provide 30 % shade cloth or install a shade cloth ring to reduce midday stress and slow further root decay. Over the next 7 days, check daily for: (i) any new soft brown roots emerging from the crown, (ii) leaf wilting or yellowing reappearance, and (iii) fruit firmness and color change; adjust watering or airflow if these signs persist.

records.label: white_mold
records.report:
Diagnosis: White Mold

1. Fruit: White, cottony mycelium blankets the entire berry, especially the green calyx, indicating active fungal growth. The soft, water-soaked surface and loss of normal gloss signal advanced decay.
2. Leaf: Several leaf edges show brown, crispy margins with a faint white fuzz, indicating infection spreading upward from the fruit. This browning and fuzz are classic signs of white mold on moist foliage.
3. Stem: The stem near the fruit is slightly darkened and water-soaked, suggesting infection has penetrated the vascular tissue, allowing spores to move upward.

To contain this infection:

1. Remove and discard all visibly infected fruit and leaves, cutting at least 2 cm (¾ in) into clean, dry soil to prevent spore spread. Sanitize shears with 70% alcohol between cuts.
2. Improve airflow by thinning crowded foliage so that each crown has at least 10 cm (4 in) of space, and water plants only at the soil line in the early morning, applying no more than 2 cm (¾ in) of water per session to keep surfaces dry.
3. Apply a 3 cm (1¼ in) layer of clean straw or pine-needle mulch under the canopy to reduce soil splash and maintain humidity below 60%. Over the next 7 days, inspect daily for new white tufts on fruit or leaves, check that mulch remains dry to the touch, and verify that morning leaf surfaces are dry within 2 hours of sunrise.
